newsitem.title: INDIA: India rice exports to suffer on currency factor.
newsitem.headline: India rice exports to suffer on currency factor.

text.p: The Indian rupee's canter up to seven month highs against a backcloth devaluations elsewhere in Asia will hurt the country's rice exports, traders and analysts said on Friday.
"The last one week there has not been any great impact," said Prem Garg, a leading New Delhi foodgrains exporter.
"But in the long run the Thai baht's effective devaluation last week will leave some impact on our rice sales," Garg told Reuters.
India has already signed contracts for rice exports this year and sales will resume only in October with the new crop.

India's main competitor as a basmati rice exporter, Pakistan, on Friday announced another devaluation of its rupee to 40.5200/7226 from 40.4600/40.6623. Meantime, the Indian rupee broke through 35.70 to the dollar to clock a seven-month high.
Also on Friday the Philippines, a rice importer, announced a de facto peso devaluation.
After the Central Bank's announcement relaxing its foreign exchange policy, the peso plunged about 11.5 percent against the dollar to a 45-month low at almost 30 pesos to the dollar.

Thailand early this month floated the baht, dropping a 13-year-old policy of pegging it to a basket of currencies, to help bolster its sagging economy hard hit by high interest rates, low exports and high imports.
Traders said with the devaluation of the baht, Thai rice would become cheaper, reducing the gap in prices of Indian and Thai rice of similar grades.
Exporters said with the change in the value of the Baht the price differential between the Indian and Thai rice would narrow down to $20-30 a tonne from the current $30-40.
They feared buyers, looking for quality rice, would not mind paying a few dollars more. Thai rice is considered superior to Indian rice varieties.
Thailand, the world's largest rice exporter, annually sells about six million tonnes of rice.
"The market is very price elastic," said Mulraj Tanna, a leading Bombay exporter. "Even traditional buyers could switch if not completely but partially (to Thai rice)."
Traders said Indian rice would also become expensive with the government increasing the price to be paid to farmers for rice purchases by eight to ten percent for the new season starting September.
Some traders said India's exports of superfine rice varieties in 1997/98 (April-March) could drop to about 1.4 million tonnes from nearly two million in 1996/97.
Tanna said Indian rice had its traditional markets in the Middle East and Africa, where Thai rice too had a market. The price differential could also take care of the higher freight costs, he said.
Anil Sharma, an agriculture-economist with the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), said a lot would depend on the extent of the depreciation of the baht.
"If the depreciation is too much then Indian exports will be priced out," Sharma said.
Traders said with the devaluation of the peso, rice imports would become costlier for Phillipines.
They said for India, Phillipines was not a large market, but Thailand could cut into its sales by increasing supplies.
Traders said demand for Indian 100 percent broken non-Basmati rice was firming up from West African countries while need for parboiled rice was growing in Nigeria.
They said about 70,000 tonnes of parboiled rice was moving to Nigeria, while nealry 60,000 tonnes were being shipped to Senegal.
They said Indian non-basmati five percent broken was quoted at $305-315 fob (free on board) per tonne, 10% broken at $290-305, 15% broken at $275-290 and 25% broken at $ 250-260.
--New Delhi newsroom (91) 11 301 2024
